4: The kit writes each result twice: the tool's status and the normalized one.
It never copies the tool's result text, because that text can name tenant objects.
Everything that is neither a pass nor a finding lands in a dispositions file, with what to do about it.
A skip for licensing needs a licensing decision.
A skip because a service was disconnected, or a result the kit is unable to evaluate, needs a fix and a re-run, or a check by hand.
A skip as not applicable needs a recorded reason, and not supported is flagged as a boundary finding.
If the export comes from a version the kit's taxonomy wasn't reviewed for, or carries a status or reason it doesn't know, the kit says so.
It counts that result as unable to evaluate, rather than guessing.
5: Every finding gets one entry, with the fields of the closure chain from Evidence, Not Verdicts: the finding and the tool version, the attack path, the owner, the dependencies, the change, the pilot, the enforcement, the test, the evidence, the residual risk, the reassessment, the weighting, and the closure decision.
The kit fills what it knows from the tool and the family table, and leaves placeholders for what a person decides.
And it never marks a finding ready for closure.
The authorizing official decides that for a plan of action and milestones item, and the assessor for an assessment finding.
6: Each test I D routes to a finding family, and each family to the page in the workbook that remediates it.
The table is from Close Before You Assess, with the evidence the guide adds for when a finding is ready for closure.
Emergency access goes to Access and Privilege, and is ready when the sign-in alert fired on a test sign-in.
Standing privilege goes to its pim chapter, and is ready when no permanent active assignment sits outside the exception register.
Device compliance goes to Devices and Endpoints, ready when a noncompliant test device is refused.
Application secrets go to Governance, Drift and Evidence.
DDoS and web application firewall findings go to the Azure Security Engineering guide.
A finding no family covers is unrouted, and goes to the Zero Trust program lead.
In release three point one point oh, the email and collaboration threat-protection tests have no family yet, so they stay unrouted and visible.
7: Two more parts of Unit 2: weighing and exceptions.
The kit sets a default priority: severity divided by effort, in buckets P one to P four.
That's design guidance, in the kit's taxonomy file.
Then the owner weighs each finding on six factors from Evidence, Not Verdicts: exploitability, blast radius, exposure, compensating controls, effort and dependency order.
The owner writes the rationale into the entry.
The register also lists each family's dependencies, so a Conditional Access finding waits for emergency access to be right.
Exceptions follow the same rule as ScubaGear's omissions.
An exception with an expiry is the see-so's decision.
One without an expiry is a standing risk acceptance, and only the authorizing official can approve it.
The kit checks each one, and marks it a governed exception, a lapsed acceptance, or a wrong approver.
